title: Influence of build-up height on residual stresses in additive repair and modification using DED-Arc with high-strength filler metals
abstract: Abstract Directed energy deposition (DED)-Arc is suitable for the hybrid additive manufacturing, modification and repair of large metal components with high deposition rates. Residual stresses and distortion are of central importance when characterizing the manufactured components and the sensitive transition area between additive manufactured (AM) component and semi-finished product. Residual stresses caused by the thermal cycles during the manufacturing process can impair the mechanical properties of the manufactured parts and can lead to component failure, especially for high-strength steels. Therefore, understanding and controlling residual stresses, when combining different base and feedstock materials, is critical to improve the quality and efficiency of the hybrid DED-Arc process. This article deals with the influence of the build-up height on the residual stress distribution of additively manufactured components with a selected base and feedstock material from commercial high-strength steels. Using a robot-assisted DED-system and a controlled short arc, AM welding experiments were carried out with close to the application parameters at working temperature (200 °C) and heat input (650 kJ/m). Five hybrid AM specimens (AM wall on upright structural steel plate) were produced using a one bead per layer strategy and selected AM-wall heights between 15 and 300 mm. The influence of the AM build height on the longitudinal residual stress in the whole hybrid AM specimen (in welding direction) was analyzed and discussed. All experiments exhibit comparable stress distributions in the area of the substrate plate up to the heat-affected zone (HAZ) and the transition zone, regardless of the building height. The height significantly influences the residual stress distribution of the deposited AM-component. Tensile residual stresses with a maximum range between 300and  400 MPa were always found in the last approx. 18 component layers (upper 40 mm). This is due to restraint of the shrinking of the top layers by the layers below. The lower layers show homogeneous residual stress distributions characterized by low compressive stresses due to the process-related tempering during the deposition of each layer on top of each other. As a result, the significant difference between the various AM build-up heights of the hybrid AM specimens is the extent (or height) of this tempered zone with low compressive stresses. These correlations contribute to the understanding of residual stress development with increasing structure height or ratio of component heights of substrate semi-finished product and AM component in hybrid additive manufacturing.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: With its Climate Law, the European Union (EU) has anchored the actions of the Green Deal in law. The declared aim is to achieve climate neutrality in the EU by 2050 in order to prevent or reduce global climate change and the resulting existential threats [ 1 ]. In addition to climate change, the current geopolitical situation also calls for the efficient use of limited resources, production capacities and skilled labor. Additive processing of high-strength materials can contribute to mastering these upcoming challenges. By substituting conventional steels with high-strength grades, the lightweight construction potential of structures can be fully utilized. In combination with the high degree of design freedom offered by additive manufacturing processes, complex geometries can be produced efficiently and with near net shape—an important contribution to the responsible use of valuable and system-relevant resources. Additive manufacturing processes can be particularly valuable and cost-effective for metal components if they are integrated into existing production routes (hybrid additive manufacturing). The hybrid additive modification or repair of semi-finished products allows the advantages of conventional and additive manufacturing to be combined to create added value [ 2 ]. With an ideal combination, hybrid AM can shorten production and throughput times, increase component complexity and production quality and positively influence the global warming potential of additively manufactured metal parts.

Due to the comparatively high deposition rates and system build volumes, DED-Arc is ideal for the hybrid additive manufacturing of large-scale mould and structural elements. Metal deposition in wire-based DED-Arc is carried out layer-wise by melting a consumable electrode using an electric arc as a heat source. It utilizes welding processes already established in joint welding, such as gas metal arc welding (GMAW), gas tungsten arc welding (GTAW) or plasma arc welding (PAW) [ 3 ,  4 ]. The respective setting variables result from the selected process parameters in combination with the individual handling system. These include travel speed, process current, voltage, wire feed rate, wire diameter, and shielding gas composition. The characteristics of the power source curve can usually be varied using additional correction factors, e.g., in the GMAW process using the arc correction and dynamic parameters. Solid wires specially adapted for DED-Arc applications have already been developed on the basis of high-strength filler materials for joint welding. These show great potential for many applications and high-strength lightweight constructions due to their extended processing window and associated production freedom.

Residual stresses are mechanical stresses in a material without the external effect of forces, moments and temperature gradients [ 5 ]. They are caused during additive manufacturing due to the transient heterogenous heating and cooling of the individual component layers in the area of the process zone as a consequence of inhomogeneous elastic and plastic deformations [ 6 ]. Similar to fusion welding, the component design, process control and material selection determine the properties and the residual stress state of additively manufactured components [ 7 ,  8 ]. The process parameters travel speed, current and voltage together with the interlayer temperature define the heat input into the component. The parameter range for the heat control (heat input, working temperature) and the cooling conditions is clearly limited, especially when processing high-strength steels to ensure the required microstructure and mechanical properties. In this context, Mueller et al. demonstrated the significant influence of process-related thermal cycles on the microstructure of high-strength filler material [ 9 ]. This demands a defined heat control, which has already been proven in own investigations for DED-Arc [ 10 ] based on comprehensive studies on process-related stresses in high-strength components for joint welding [ 11 ]. Mueller et al. showed the influence of heat input and interlayer temperature on the mechanical-technological properties of the final component in additive manufacturing experiments with a high-strength solid steel wire [ 12 ]. High heat inputs and interlayer temperatures led to reduced yield strengths. Reindl et al. investigated the influence of substrate preheating and in-situ cooling on component properties using a water-cooled build platform [ 13 ]. By directly influencing the cooling behavior, it was possible to specifically affect the microstructure in the transition area between the substrate and the AM component, as well as the layer geometry. Various studies on the DED process focus on process-related stresses and their significant reduction through optimized additive and mechanical processing steps [ 14 ,  15 ]. For example, high interlayer temperatures are recommended for AM production to reduce residual stresses and distortion [ 16 ]. Own investigations also show a distinct influence of the process-related heat control on the resulting residual stresses. In tests with high-strength solid steel wire feedstock, high heat inputs and interlayer temperatures led to lower residual stresses in the additively manufactured components [ 17 ]. In addition to the process power parameters, correlations for heat control, residual stresses and path planning could also be identified. The spatial arrangement of the tool paths (deposition strategy and position) influences the heat input into the component and thus also the formation of the seam cross-section. In their work, Koehler et al. showed the significant influence of the additive filling strategy on the temperature distribution and ultimately on the cooling behavior of aluminum components [ 18 ]. Furthermore, they were able to achieve a more homogeneous temperature distribution in the component using a special filling strategy (s-pattern), which can have a positive effect on porosity, residual stresses, and microstructure. In addition to the process parameters and the deposition strategy, the build position and torch orientation also have a significant influence on the seam geometry and component properties. Hensel et al. compared the seam widths and surface waviness of straight walls produced in different construction positions [ 19 ]. A significant increase in component surface waviness could be observed when working in horizontal position. Furthermore, they found a correlation between the effective wall width and the wall waviness. Such geometric relationships must also be considered when evaluating component properties and residual stresses in the context of component integrity.

A change in component geometry affects the cooling behavior of the component and the load-bearing cross-sections. This affects not only the generation of residual stress in the process zone, but also the residual stress equilibrium at the component level and the stiffness ratios between the substrate and the AM component. Various research groups have already investigated the influence of component design on the evolution of residual stress profiles. Huang et al. focused on the residual stress distribution in wall and pipe structures made of austenitic steel [ 20 ]. Using FEA, they showed that for both geometries, the largest residual stresses in terms of magnitude occurred several layers below the last layer. Furthermore, they observed a quasi-stable tensile-compressive-tensile longitudinal residual stress pattern from the bottom to the top of the components. Components below this height only experience residual tensile stresses in the process direction. Ahmad et al. also investigated the influence of geometry in [ 21 ], examining the effect of selected build-up strategies on residual stresses in aluminum components. They investigated single bead, parallel path, and oscillation path and the effect of interlayer hammer peening and changes in interlayer temperature. After removing the base plate, the wall with the oscillating path planning showed the lowest residual stresses. The highest longitudinal residual stresses were found at the wall with the parallel path planning. All walls exhibited compressive stresses in the middle area. Furthermore, the interlayer layer hammer peening had a significant stress-reducing effect on the manufactured walls. Sun et al. simulated the influence of build height and clamping conditions on DED arc with aluminum [ 22 ] using FEA. This revealed compressive stresses in the final layer at a build-up height of 20 mm or more. Furthermore, a significant influence of the clamping system used on the resulting longitudinal stress state was observed. Overall, the effect of the building height and the clamping system on the transversal residual stresses were small.

The use of high-strength steels undoubtedly offers great economic advantages, especially in hybrid additive manufacturing using DED-Arc. The process-related residual stresses and material-related degradation caused by generative manufacturing steps result in high process engineering requirements due to the low elongation reserves. There have been no systematic studies to date, particularly in connection with the reliable production of a stress-compliant connection between the substrate and the additively manufactured structure during component modification of high-strength steel components. Due to the special microstructure of high-strength steels combined with low elongation reserves, high residual stresses should be avoided, especially in the transition areas of hybrid manufactured components. In this complex field, the present work deals with the influence of the build-up height on the distribution of the process-induced residual stresses in high-strength metal component. Own investigations using X-ray diffraction analyses (XRD) show that DED-Arc of high-strength steels cause high residual stresses, particularly in the process direction of the component. Furthermore, the resulting residual stresses vary significantly with changing component complexity and dimensions [ 23 ]. By increasing the height of the component (from 20 to 50 mm) by applying additional layers, longitudinal residual stresses could be significantly reduced. These investigations provided initial insights into the influence of the component height on the residual stress state on a small scale. In this work, these initial observations are systematically analyzed on larger components and over broader height variations than in [ 23 ] in order to clarify the influence of building height on the residual stress state of DED-Arc manufactured high-strength AM components.

sections.heading: Material and specimen manufacturing
paragraphs:
The high-strength fine-grained structural steel S690QL (material no. 1.8928) in accordance with DIN EN 10025–6 (area of application e.g. mobile crane construction) with a sheet thickness of 20 mm was used as the substrate material for the experimental investigations [ 24 ]. Table  1  shows the mechanical properties and the chemical composition of the selected materials. The chemical composition of the substrate was determined using an optical emission spectrometer (OES). Further information is taken from the data sheets/delivery conditions of the steel manufacturers. The substrates were annealed and cleaned before additive modification in order to remove all existing residual stresses. The stress relief annealing consisted of a 4-h heating up to 580 °C, a holding time period of 6 h and cooling to room temperature over 14 h. Subsequent cleaning was carried out using a pickling solution consisting of water and hydrochloric acid. In addition, a voestalpine boehler welding 3Dprint AM 80 HD (10NiMnMoCr8-7–6) with a diameter of  d  = 1.2 mm was selected as the feedstock metal.
 Table 1 Chemical composition in wt.% (Fe balanced) and mechanical properties of the materials according to OES and datasheet Material Chemical composition Mechanical properties C Si Mn Cr Mo Ni Yield strength R p0.2  in MPa Tensile strength R m  in MPa Elongation A 5  in % Substrate S690QL 0.14 0.30 1.15 0.30 0.17 0.10  ≥ 690  ≥ 770  ≥ 14 Wire AM 80 HD* 0.09 0.40 1.70 0.35 0.60 2.00 825 960 20 * Datasheet voestalpine boehler welding

A KUKA KR 6 robot system with KR C2 controller and a Fronius iWave 400i AC/DC welding system were used for additive manufacturing of the specimens. In addition to that, a GMA welding process (135) with controlled short arc and reversing wire movement (CMT) was chosen (see Fig.  1 ). The specimens were manufactured on a 20 °C water-cooled work table. Preheating to the working temperature specified in the experimental design was done inductively. The tests were carried out with free-shrinking clamping in the building direction on substrate plates made of S690QL with a length of 170 mm, a thickness of 20 mm and a height of 80 mm. In accordance with the specifications of the experimental design, 5 walls with a length of 150 mm, a thickness of 10 mm and varying component heights were additively manufactured from voestalpine boehler welding 3Dprint AM 80 HD filler metal. Specimens with component heights of 15 mm, 50 mm, 100 mm, 150 mm, and 300 mm were produced for the stage termination test. The manufacturing process was carried out using a one seam per layer strategy with alternating deposit direction. Figure  2  shows the experimental design and all relevant geometrical features. Fig. 1 Experimental equipment consisting of a KUKA KR 6 robot system with welding torch, Fronius iWave 400i AC/DC power source, water-cooled workbench and Micro Epsilon TIM 8 thermal camera for monitoring process and interlayer temperatures Fig. 2 Basic test geometry and the experimental design (no.1 to no. 5) to determine the influence of the building height on the residual stress state of hybrid AM components

The production strategy was maintained in terms of path planning, preheating and interlayer temperature (200 °C) as well as heat input (650 kJ/m). These parameters were selected based on own investigations into the influence of the manufacturing strategy on AM walls. The selected heat input and interlayer temperature enabled the production of 10 mm thick walls with one seam per layer and moderate cooling rates within the manufacturer's recommended range. Only a variation of the building height according to the experimental design was carried out within levels 1 to 5. The first layer was produced at 80% of the respective process speed in order to achieve proper bonding. An overview of the constant and varied process parameters can be seen in Table  2 .
 Table 2 Constant process parameters and system settings for analyzing the influence of the building height on the residual stress state Welding machine: Fronius iWave 400i AC/DC Contact tube to workpiece distance: 16 mm Characteristic: Steel, CMT 4348 dynamic Shielding gas: ISO 14175–M21-ArC-20 Wire feed rate: ≈ 4 m/min Feedstock material: voestalpine 3Dprint AM 80 HD Dynamics/arc length:  + 5/−5 Wire diameter: 1.2 mm Travel speed: ≈ 21 cm/min Substrate metal/thickness: DIN EN 10025–6 S690QL Mean current/voltage ≈ 137 A/≈ 13 V Substrate thickness: 20 mm

sections.heading: Cooling time and residual stress measurement
paragraphs: The start time of the automatic measurement was always the time at which the welding torch reached the position  x  = 135 mm along the tool path, 15 mm before the end of each bead. The end time was always the time of cooling to 450 °C. The so-called cooling time Δ t x-450 °C  results from the layer-by-layer subtraction of the two time stamps  t x  and  t 450 °C , see formula 1 and Fig.  3 . In this test arrangement, thermographic temperature measurement allows measurement, recording, evaluation and process control on the basis of maximum temperatures without having to define the location of the evaluation in detail. This is a decisive advantage compared to pyrometric measurement methods. Furthermore, global process-related heat treatment can be mapped better compared to a position-static evaluation. Fig. 3 Determination of the cooling time using thermography,  a:  snapshot of the process during production of the last component layer 135 mm after start position,  b:  snapshot of the process after cooling down to 450 °C

The residual stress measurements were carried out using X-ray diffraction (XRD) [ 26 ,  27 ]. The mobile X-ray diffractometer G3 from the company Stresstech was used to determine the residual stresses near the surface with a penetration depth of approx. 5 μm. Before the measurements, the diffractometer was calibrated with an Fe reference sample. Table  3  shows the settings and specifications of the X-ray diffractometer used. The principle sketch and measuring procedure are shown in Fig.  4 .
 Table 3 Device specification and setting for residual stress measurement using XRD (sin2ψ method) Radiation: CrKα Tube power: 30 kV/6.7 mA Collimator: 2 mm Detector: linear solid state Diffraction line: {211} α ψ -tilting: 0 to ± 45° ψ -steps: 10 Measuring time: 8 s per point Fig. 4 Residual stress measurement using XRD, left: schematic drawing, middle: hybrid AM component in the measuring device, right: measuring track in building direction along the component symmetry

The measurement of the longitudinal residual stresses in the direction of deposition was carried out layer by layer on the outer surface of the component in building direction along the axis of symmetry/center line, cf. Fig  4 . A distance of 10 mm between each measuring line was chosen for the residual stress mapping.

sections.heading: Results and discussion
paragraphs: By varying the component height, a total of 5 hybrid AM walls were produced. Figure  5  shows the manufacturing result for the 5 different building heights. All specimens shown were produced with identical process parameters and the same fabrication strategy, cf. Fig  2  and Table  2 . Surface and seam quality are comparable. The set process parameters resulted in a relatively constant layer cross-section with a layer height of  h  = 2.2 mm and a layer width of  b  = 10 mm for all walls. The upstream substrate cleaning, tempering to working temperature and application of the first component layer at a reduced process speed (80%) resulted in crack-free bonding of the AM component to the substrate in all 5 test cases; an important and necessary prerequisite for comparing the residual stresses with each other (verified by dye penetration test). Fig. 5 Manufacturing results for analyzing the influence of the build-up height on the longitudinal residual stresses of hybrid AM components with the build heights  h C  15, 50, 100, 150 and 300 mm

Apart from the initial adaptation of the process parameters for the first bonding layer, the additive manufacturing of all the walls shown was successful without any manual or algorithmic adaptation of the process parameters or the manufacturing strategy during the building phase.

Figure  6  shows cooling time Δ t X-450 °C  as a function of the component height  h C  for the 5 hybrid AM components produced. First of all, it is noticeable that all curves lie on top of each other and end at different heights. It is understandable that they terminate at different heights, as the walls only differ in this geometric parameter (nature of the stage termination experiment). The fact that they lie on top of each other is another important prerequisite for being able to compare the measured residual stresses with each other meaningful, as all experiments were carried out under thermally comparable and reproducible conditions. Furthermore, two characteristic areas can be identified on the basis of the measured cooling times. In the first so-called transition area, the cooling time Δ t X-450 °C  increases steadily from approx. 12 s after the first layer to approx. 35 s at a component height  h C  of approx. 35 mm (16 layers). This can be explained by the fact that the component, which is initially only preheated to 200 °C, accumulates thermal energy due to the cyclical process-related heating. As a result, cooling to 450 °C slows down slowly from 12 to 35 s layer by layer over the initial 35 mm. This is followed by the transition to the thermal stable zone 2, accompanied by stabilization of the cooling time Δ t x-450 °C  to approx. 35 s. Once in this area, the cooling values show only a very slight increase. Fig. 6 The cooling time  Δt X-450 °C  as a function of the component height  h C  for the 5 hybrid AM components produced

After exceeding a component height  h C  of approx. 35 mm, an equilibrium was established between the thermal energy supplied by the process and the thermal energy dissipated to the environment and the substrate. Above the transition height of  h C  ≈ 35 mm, the further deposition of component layers only showed a very small effect on the cooling conditions of the hybrid AM wall within the investigated parameter range of the experimental design. The transition height depends on the cooling behavior of the component. Nevertheless, Mueller et al. obtained comparable curves with the characteristic two zones in their interlayer temperature-controlled experiments [ 12 ]. This observation raises the question of whether comparable patterns can also be verified for the residual stress state with regard to the component height, as this is significantly influenced by the cooling behavior, c.f. [ 23 ].

For the analysis, the residual stresses were determined in all three spatial directions. Only the longitudinal residual stresses in the welding (longitudinal) direction showed significant quantities and gradients. Figure  7  shows an exemplary residual stress distribution in the longitudinal direction for the hybrid AM specimen with an AM height of 100 mm in comparison with the stress-relieved annealed initial substrate steel plate, exemplarily as a profile along the axis of symmetry (right) and as map on an area of 180 mm × 30 mm near the axis of symmetry (left). The initial substrate exhibits of course a residual stress state with a value of approximately 0 MPa. In terms of the residual stress distribution of the hybrid AM component, a bending moment or stress arises in the AM part, along with a corresponding bending stress in the substrate. The substrate shows zero crossings (neutral axis) of the residual stresses and the AM part zero crossings in the first layers and in case of a height of over 40 mm also in the approx. last 15 layers. The residual stress distribution can be described by starting from the bottom of the substrate and moving upwards towards the top layer of the AM part. Initially, the bottom of the substrate exhibits significant tensile residual stresses. These stresses then gradually shift linearly towards compressive residual stresses as the first neutral axis is crossed. The compressive residual stresses increase almost linearly, reaching their peak in the upper region of the substrate. Then, the compressive residual stresses begin to decrease almost linear till reaching the second neutral axis at the beginning of the AM part. Up to a component height of approx. 60 mm, the residual stress varies slightly around 0 MPa with a minimal tendency toward compressive residual stresses for higher layers. This is due to the repeated heat treatment of the subsequent weld layers, incorporating a relaxation of the previously induced residual stresses. At a component height of approximately 60 mm, the residual stresses shift to tensile residual stresses, which increase consistently due to the restriction of shrinkage in the deposited layers without repeated tempering. The uppermost layers of the AM component show a significant decrease in tensile residual stresses. This localized effect is explained by a solid phase transformation. According to well-established theories, this type of stress relief, known as transformation-induced residual stress, results from restricted volumetric expansion during cooling as the material transitions from an austenitic phase to a bainitic or martensitic microstructure [ 23 ,  28 ]. This mechanism, combined with the lower degree of restraint towards the upper layers, contributes to decreases in residual stress levels, both locally [ 29 ] and globally [ 16 ,  30 ]. Similar results were obtained for the same materials when tested with a different geometry and varying heat inputs [ 31 ]. Fig. 7 Visualization of the longitudinal residual stresses in travelling direction as for the central point experiment (stage 3), left: Residual stress map of an area of 180 mm × 30 mm, right: Longitudinal residual stresses along the axis of symmetry – initial state vs. final state after AM

The comparative visualization of longitudinal residual stress profiles with their error bands as a function of the build-up height  h C  is shown in Fig.  8 . No significant differences in the residual stress distribution are observable in the area of the substrate plate till the HAZ for the specimens higher than 15 mm. A negative residual stress gradient with a comparable magnitude can be recognized for all building heights. The 15 mm specimen shows a significantly lower negative longitudinal residual stress gradient in this area. This is in good agreement with the ratio of build-up to substrate geometry. The low tensile force of the few deposited layers correlates with a reduced bending moment in the substrate plate. Further difference can be seen in the area of the HAZ. Larger build heights correlate with lower residual compressive stress in the HAZ. This can presumably be explained by the position of the neutral axis of the substrate component system, which is shifted upwards in building direction at higher component heights, accompanied by a reduction in residual compressive stresses due to superimposed bending stresses. Furthermore, positive stress gradients with an increase in the longitudinal residual stresses to over 200 MPa can be seen in the upper area of the AM walls. This gradient is found in all specimens within the last 40 mm or 18 component layers. The maximum longitudinal residual stresses could be identified in specimen no. 2 ( h C  = 50 mm) with tensile residual stresses of approx. 380 MPa. Likewise, almost all experiments show a slight decrease in tension in the last 1 to 3 layers. The middle area of the AM component between the substrate plate and the upper positive stress gradient is characterized by relatively homogeneous, moderate residual compressive stresses. However, this can only be seen in the specimens with a component height  h C  > 40 mm (> 18 layers), as only in these cases sufficient layers were applied to obtain the relaxing effect of the process-related heat treatment. This also explains the direct transition from the negative to the positive residual stress gradient in specimens with a component height  h C  lower than 40 mm resp. 18 layers. Fig. 8 Influence of the construction height  h C  on the longitudinal residual stress state  σ E X (z)  in the traveling direction for straight walls

With regard to the distribution of the longitudinal residual stresses, 3 characteristic sectors can be identified for the building heights investigated according to the experimental design, cf. Fig  7 . Sector 1 is located between the bottom side of the substrate plate and the beginning of the HAZ and is characterized by a negative residual stress gradient, which is comparable in gradient and magnitude for all specimens with a building height  h C  over 15 mm. Sector 3 comprises the last approx. 40 mm resp. 18 component layers of the AM component and shows a significant positive residual stress gradient with a minimal drop within the last 2 to 3 layers. Sector 2 is located between these two sectors and is characterized by relatively homogeneously distributed low residual compressive stresses. The spatial extent of this sector 2 is therefore dependent on the height of the structure. Distribution and magnitude of the longitudinal residual stresses in sector 3 are largely independent of the building height. In this upper part of the component, the tempering effect of the remaining layers is insufficient to effectively relax the process-induced residual tensile stresses. As a result, the characteristic process-induced residual stress gradient remains in the upper layers. The extent of this gradient in the build-up direction is therefore primarily dependent on the number of thermal cycles or layers required for adequate residual stress relaxation. In GMAW-based additive manufacturing, layer height, seam cross-section, wire feed rate and heat input are closely linked. A variation in heat input (e.g., by reducing the layer height via the wire feed rate) always affects the residual stress distribution. In particular, it influences the number of thermal cycles required for effective residual stress relaxation and the extent of the residual stress gradient in the build-up direction, but not the qualitative residual stress distribution. This observation is in good agreement with the results of Sarmast et al., who were able to measure comparable residual stress gradients and sectors in similar specimen geometries with different process parameters and materials [ 32 ]. Further growth of the AM geometry shifts zone 3 in the direction of build. Figure  9  clearly shows the right drift of sector 3 depending on the building height  h C  from specimen no. 1 to no. 5. Fig. 9 Right shift of the positive gradient of the longitudinal residual stresses in the upper area of the wall geometry as a function of the building height  h C

In addition to that, the longitudinal residual stresses also reveal a tendency with regard to the maxima. In general, higher longitudinal residual stresses occur with smaller build-up heights  h C  and vice versa, see Figs.  8  and  9 . This has also been described by K. Wandtke et al. in [ 23 ] for other specimen geometries and lower height variation and was explained by the increasing influence of the buildup AM geometry and the associated reduction in the effect of the substrate stiffness. With increased component height, the shrinkage-inhibiting effect of the rigid substrate is reduced, particularly in the upper area of the AM geometry, where the residual stress maxima are located.

sections.heading: Summary and conclusions
paragraphs: This study focused on the influence of the build-up height on the distribution of longitudinal residual stresses in hybrid AM components made of high-strength materials. For this purpose, AM walls with constant production parameters, strategies and varying component heights were generated in a stage termination experiment with free shrinkage onto a high-strength substrate. The following conclusions can be drawn from the cooling rate and residual stress measurements and results presented: The cooling behavior of the walls analyzed in the investigated parameter matrix can be described in 2 phases/zones, a transient and a stable phase. At the beginning of additive manufacturing, the analyzed cooling time increased from approx. 12 s to 35 s at a component height of 35 mm (transient phase). After exceeding this so-called transition height, the further deposition of component layers only showed a very small influence on the analyzed cooling time, which was only subject to a slight increase for the rest of the manufacturing process (stable phase). All specimens except the lowest with a build-up height of  h c  = 15 mm showed comparable negative residual stress gradients in the substrate up to the HAZ. All specimens except the lowest with a build-up height of  h c  = 15 mm showed moderate residual compressive stresses in the transition zone of approx. −100 MPa. Due to the compressive stress loaded HAZ, there is no risk of cold cracking in the transition zone between semi-finished product and AM component. All specimens reveal positive gradients in longitudinal residual stresses in the upper 40 mm range and a slight residual stress decrease towards the top layer, regardless of the building height. The position of this positive stress gradient depends on the component height and was always located in the last 40 mm (18 layers) of the analyzed specimens. Between the positive residual stress gradient in the upper area of the component and the HAZ, a comparatively homogeneous low-level compressive stress range was formed. The extension of this area in the build-up direction is dependent on the component height.

This study is part of a running research project on the properties of hybrid additive components and processes. It aims the stress optimized hybrid additive manufacturing of high-strength components and the necessary recommendations for application. In addition, the effects of the welding assembly of DED-printed components on the local and global residual stress state of welded assemblies are to be comprehensively and systematically clarified in future investigations.
